extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, students, and general readers interested in collaborative mathematical research projects
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive norms for participating in or organizing a Polymath-style massively collaborative mathematics project: selecting problems, contributing via online threads, role expectations, and publication practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project goal / problem selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve important and difficult mathematical problems by coordinating many mathematicians to communicate with each other on finding the best route to the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The project typically begins with choosing an important unsolved mathematical problem (original research). Examples: Polymath1 targeted a new combinatorial proof of the density Hales–Jewett theorem; Polymath8 targeted improving bounds for gaps between primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution type — partial ideas and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were asked to post partial ideas and partial progress toward a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions need not be full solutions; incremental insights, partial results, heuristics, or calculations are appropriate. Gowers explicitly invited readers to post partial ideas in blog comments as the primary mode of contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation venue / communication medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blog comments and online collaboration (central blogs, threads) as the primary coordination and discussion space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polymath activity has been carried out in comment threads on blogs (e.g., Gowers's and Tao's blogs) and on a central Polymath Project blog / hubs. Multiple parallel threads on different blogs can coexist and coordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project structure — threaded/subproject decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourse can split into multiple threads focusing on different goals (e.g., combinatorial proof vs. bounds calculations) or into named subprojects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polymath1 grew two main threads with different focuses; Polymath8 split into Polymath8a and Polymath8b with distinct but related aims. Organizers may create subprojects to pursue specific subgoals or techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant roles and eligibility (Crowdmath variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdmath projects are aimed at high school and college students with advanced background; older participants are welcomed as mentors and encouraged not to post solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For outreach/educational variants, students from around the world with an advanced math background are encouraged to participate; mentors should guide but refrain from posting complete solutions so students can learn from the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and publication practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative outputs are often published under the pseudonym 'D. H. J. Polymath'; journal and archive practices may differ about listing real names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several Polymath projects produced papers published under the Polymath pseudonym (arXiv versions often use the pseudonym); some journals required editors/authors to use real names even when the arXiv/journal table of contents referenced contributors differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected outputs and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Polymath projects aim to produce mathematical results such as new proofs, improved bounds, and research papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Polymath1 produced at least two papers (Density Hales–Jewett results); Polymath8a/8b produced improved bounds on prime gaps and published papers. Even when a project does not fully solve a stated problem (Polymath5 initially), it can contribute key ideas used later by individual researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative / temporal nature of collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects proceed iteratively, possibly continuing work after an initial declaration of 'probably solved' and lasting weeks to months or being periodically revived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polymath1 continued for months after an initial seven-week period; Polymath5 was active in 2010 and briefly revived in 2012. Expect ongoing refinement and follow-up even after main progress is announced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and inclusivity principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Polymath model is a crowdsourcing/open-science approach: online collaboration allows broad participation in solving math problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment was explicitly framed as 'massively collaborative mathematics' and 'using an online collaboration to solve any math problem', encouraging wide participation and diverse contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational / outreach objective for Crowdmath
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdmath adapts the Polymath approach to create opportunities for the upcoming generation of math and science researchers by focusing on students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowdmath projects select original research/unsolved problems appropriate for advanced high-school and college students, with mentoring structures to foster learning rather than simply soliciting solutions.
